Elias had not spoken a word in three years. The silence of the North Cape lighthouse was not empty; it was heavy, a physical weight that pressed against his eardrums and settled in his bones. He was a man carved from the same granite as the cliff, weathered by salt and wind, his eyes the pale, washed-out blue of a winter sea.

Every evening, as the sun bled out over the horizon, Elias climbed the one hundred and twelve steps to the lantern room. His knees ached, a dull, persistent throb that served as a metronome for his existence. He lit the great Fresnel lens, a crystal heart that captured the flame and threw it into the dark, slicing the night into rhythmic, golden wedges. *Click. Hiss. Glow.* The ritual was his prayer, his penance, and his only connection to the world beyond the glass.

The storms came often here, violent and hungry. They battered the tower, shaking the very foundation, but Elias remained steady. He watched the waves crash against the rocks below, white foam exploding like shattered bone. In the eye of the gale, he would sometimes see a ship, a tiny, trembling speck of light struggling against the chaos. He would adjust the lens, focusing the beam with a precision that felt almost supernatural, guiding them safely past the jagged teeth of the reef.

One night, a young fisherman’s boat was caught in a sudden squall. The light from the lighthouse cut through the rain, a beacon of hope in the void. Elias watched, his heart hammering against his ribs, until the boat turned, its lights aligning with his beam. As it disappeared into the safety of the harbor, Elias felt a strange, quiet warmth spread through his chest. He didn’t smile, but the tension in his shoulders eased.
